items.title: How a Frontier Team Can Help Your Company Keep Up With AI
items.content: You need a frontier team. Here's why. Every single person in your company is caught in this dilemma. Do I get my work done or do I stay up to date with AI and figure out what all these new tools and workflows mean for what work I should do? That's just crazy. It's so hard to figure out. Every single company is struggling with this right now. Because, I mean, on the one hand, you could ignore the frontier and that'll probably work for a little while until you get disrupted by some agent native version of your product that you didn't see coming. Or you can keep up with the frontier and just chase shiny objects and never build anything that lasts. The reason why you need a frontier team is it separates things out. So you get this nice separation of concerns where you're both keeping up with what's going on on the frontier and you're actually getting your work done. And I had my co-host, Natalia. Welcome, Natalia. Hey, Dan. Good to be here. Who is our head of enterprise AI adoption. Come in and do a little bit of digging into our Frontier team. So we've been running the Frontier team at Every for, I guess, a couple of months now. And it has been kind of transformative. And I think Natalia is one of the best people to come in and take a peek and be like, what are we actually doing? So actually, I might turn the tables a little bit to you because it was your idea to have a frontier team. Yeah. I mean, yeah, the frontier team, I think has been a huge unlock and it's because of this separation that, that I've been talking about. I think there's so many people at every like me who just love playing with new things and that's super important. But if that's all you're doing, then you're, you're not going to make progress as a business. Like you actually do need to go execute on products and services, things that people can rely on. And it felt like we needed to choose one or the other. Yeah. either just constantly be playing with new stuff or make a product that we just build once and then we add features to and we support forever. And the Frontier team was in a sort of an attempt to say, okay, what if we take all the people like me who love all the new stuff and we just unleash us to just run experiments? And at the low end, the experiments are just, they're just really good content. They just teach us something interesting and they become good tweets or YouTube videos or anything like that. And then on the high end, they get pushed up from the frontier into the products that we build, into the services that we offer, without the rest of the company feeling like they always had to be paying attention to every single model that drops in every single new experiment that we're running. So I felt like it's allowed me and the other people on the frontier team the space to just figure out what the future looks like without forcing that on the rest of the company until it's actually ready for them to pay attention to it. Now, one of the things that you seem to have figured out pretty early in the formation of the Frontier team is that you wanted to have both pirates and architects. Can you describe what that is? I think there's two archetypes that work really well together, pirates and architects. Pirates are people like me who are just like, I just want to go really fast and I'm going to do stuff that's kind of be a little bit sloppy, but I'm going to try like a billion things in the space of a couple days. And I'm going to figure out what's useful. but it's gonna be a mess. Architects are people who are really good at being like, there's a whole big messy thing what would it look like to compress it a little bit and form it into a shape that actually works, that we can actually use? Because what we try to do on the Frontier team is we're experimenting with lots of stuff. Most of that stuff gets thrown out. And some of it ends up getting pushed into the rest of the team to see if the rest of the team likes it. And at that point, there's a po…

items.title: MOFCOM's New Rules and the Future of Chinese AI
items.content: In the AI race thus far, openness has been China’s secret sauce. As fast followers to the frontier, Chinese AI companies have gained trust by publicizing their weights and architectures. And at the cost of revenue, they have achieved global adoption, brand recognition, and a truly competitive dynamic with American labs. Last week, China’s Ministries of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Science and Technology (MOST) jointly proposed expanding China’s catalogue of export-controlled technologies, with most of the proposed regulations taking aim at subsets of China’s AI industry. Regulators will spend a month taking comments on the draft before anything becomes law, but we can already learn a ton from this announcement in its current form. Does Beijing want to hold back the tides of open models? Why is MOFCOM writing these rules now, and what does this say about the Chinese government’s appetite for AI-enabled risks versus growth? To find out, we spent three days poring over the draft regulations — so you don’t have to! What’s ahead: How these rules came to be — and how this draft is already affecting the Chinese AI industry; What the proposed rules mean for frontier models, chip design, memory, cybersecurity, AI content detection, and even China’s minority languages; Who actually decides which export licenses get approved, and the balance of power between provincial and central authorities; What these rules tell us about Beijing’s expectations for AI development. The 40 proposed additions in Announcement 48, split across AI, photovoltaics, and biomedicine. Today, we’re just focusing on the AI-related regulations, but a future piece tackling everything else — from this announcement’s proposed restrictions on PV cells and gene therapies, to other recent announcements on port dredgers and tunnel borers — is in the works! items.title: The Case for DUV Controls
items.content: Saif Khan makes his ChinaTalk debut. He is perhaps my favorite example of posting-to-policy that I’ve seen over the course of my time following Washington. Saif wrote some truly excellent deep dives into AI and semiconductors during his time at CSET, then went into the NSC and Commerce in the early-to-mid 2020s, across both the Biden and Trump II administrations, to help manifest the export control regulatory regime we have today. He is now out of government and launching the Center for Technology and Statecraft , an IFP -affiliated think tank, which is already producing excellent, grounded, technical, forward-looking work that will certainly shape many an AI policy discussion in the years to come. We discuss: Why Saif started a new think tank, and the value of deep, forward-looking policy research in an AI world moving at breakneck speed; CTS’s landmark DUV report, which projects that stopping tool exports today could leave China producing roughly 100x fewer AI chips than the US by the mid-2030s, making DUV controls the US’s most consequential lever over the AI balance; How rigorous research actually translates into government policy, and why think tank experience is valuable before working in government; Robotics as the next frontier of US-China AI competition, and the security vs. diffusion mindsets shaping AI policy; How AI is changing policy research itself, the challenge of bringing AI into government, and what AI-driven economic and social change could mean for humans. Plus, why everyone should read Lu Xun, why AI might socialize like insects, and AI-nannying. Listen now on your favorite podcast app ! Why Another Think Tank? Jordan Schneider: Saif Khan, at long last, welcome to ChinaTalk. Why does the world need another think tank? What is the appetite right now for evidence-based policy? items.title: Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar
items.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust.  Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It…

items.title: How we contain Claude across products
items.content: Twelve months ago, we'd have rejected out of hand the idea of granting Claude access sufficient to take down an internal Anthropic service. Today that level of access is routine, and Anthropic developers are more productive for it. The risk of these deployments has two components: how likely a failure is, and how much damage one could do. Progress on safeguards and model training has steadily driven down the first; the second—the theoretical blast radius—only grows as capabilities and access expand. Yet as agents become capable of doing work that once required a person or even a team, the cost of not deploying grows large enough that the risk-reward calculation tips heavily toward adoption, as long as products can be made safe. The engineering question becomes how to cap the blast radius. When bounds can be placed on the relative damage of an autonomous agent—such as through control over its environment—high-utility capabilities can motivate deployment. Claude Mythos Preview is an example of a model whose blast radius was deemed too high to ship in April 2026. However, we expect broader release of models with similar levels of capability to become appropriate as defenders harden critical systems and safeguards mature—even though some risk will always remain. Model capability is an important factor in the total risk of an agent’s deployment. There are broadly two ways to do this. The first is to supervise the agent’s behavior via a human-in-the-loop. Claude Code previously protected against agents taking unintended actions by asking users for permission at each turn. Theoretically that works, but we’ve found the approach to be fallible. Our telemetry showed users approved roughly 93% of permission prompts. The more approvals a user sees, the less attention they pay to each, becoming over time much less diligent in their supervision. We recently built Claude Code auto mode, which automates safer approvals in order to reduce this approval fatigue. Still, vulnerab…

items.title: Crossing the Threshold: How OpenAI and Anthropic Approach Autonomy and Safety in Financial Agents
items.content: OpenAI’s Joseph Kim talks about the threshold phenomenon at AIE NY today. One of the key themes at the AI Engineer New York conference this week was how to balance agent autonomy with security and safety . Both frontier labs and financial firms focused on this issue in their presentations this week. The main lesson: safe autonomy depends on where you put controls and human judgment , rather than how many restrictions you impose. Sponsor: Build shopping into your agent with shop.dev Adding commerce to an agent usually means rebuilding search and checkout from scratch. shop.dev gives you a single API for shopping in any agent or app. One connection gives you access to over a billion products with current price and availability, instant sign in with Shop, and one-tap Shop Pay checkout that happens right in the conversation. It’s open to any developer, with no account or key needed to try it. → Try shop.dev today Joseph Kim , Head of ChatGPT for Financial Services at OpenAI, gave a keynote at AIE New York today. (We also did a special podcast with Kim, which will be released shortly.) He talked about reliability and a “threshold of usefulness,” which he said is “the point where a model becomes capable and reliable enough to save you time.” Kim argued that ever-growing model capability will soon take financial analysts over the threshold and allow them to delegate more work to agents. He made some specific predictions about AI’s role in finance in 2027. Not only will the financial industry rely less on Excel and PowerPoint next year, he claimed, but agents will be good enough to do “investment idea generation and trading.” The “rising tide” of model capabilities is also leading to better traceability . “In finance, you need to be able to check where a number came from and understand the context around it,” said Kim. “We wanted that review to be a natural part of the [ChatGPT for Fi…

items.title: 10 Takeaways from Q3
items.content: AI, China, defense, national security, supply chains, the Protestant roots of Kim Il-sung’s Messiah complex , the lethality of hydrofluoric acid, and horseback archery in Kyrgyzstan. It’s been a productive Q3. Here are some of the things we learned and why we think they matter. The ChinaTalk team is growing! We’ve welcomed Quinn Ennis , our newest full-time analyst, and Michael Palmer , who has been doing great work behind the scenes on video and audio! China and AI What does Liang Wenfeng actually believe? The DeepSeek Thesis reconstructs DeepSeek’s strategy from leaked minutes of a four-hour meeting between Liang Wenfeng and investors. For Liang, general intelligence is the only problem worth solving — products can wait, because “once truly generalized and convincingly superior intelligence arrives, creating to-C and to-B products will be trivial.” Why it matters: This is a rare window into the worldview of one of the most important people in Chinese AI. Liang is all-in on AGI rather than diverting focus toward commercializing current AI capabilities, and he’s betting that open models and Chinese chips can get him there. Why are Chinese AI researchers so skeptical of American AI safety? In How Chinese AI Radicalizes , Irene traces an unsettling development: some Chinese researchers are increasingly concluding that American AI-safety rhetoric is just a form of technological containment. DeepSeek researcher Liu Shengyu’s viral essay argues that frontier AI should be broadly accessible rather than controlled by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI (and yes, he mentions Hitler). In short, American AI safety rhetoric is backfiring in China. Why it matters: If Chinese AI researchers interpret American safety arguments through the lens of anti-China containment, genuine US-China cooperation becomes harder, just as increasingly capable AI makes cooperation more important. items.title: Dyna-2: General Purpose Physical Agents with Hour-Long Autonomy — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
items.content: Watch along AIE NYC and join us at AIE CODE in SF next month! This episode includes a live demo of the Taku robot that is best enjoyed on YouTube . Last month, Dyna made waves by announcing Dyna-2 , a world-action model pre-trained on one million hours of human video, claiming several new scaling laws on human data across four orders of magnitude . They have now followed up the model with a physical robot agent, Dyna-2.1 , that has to be seen to be believed: In his talk at AIE this year, Jason talked about how the real challenge for robotics in the real world is reliable, long-horizon autonomy , and how Dyna got its models to a 99.4% success rate folding restaurant napkins for 24 hours straight, including recovering after it pulled over the whole stack. From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung , Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. In this episode, Dyna Robotics co-founder and Chief Scientist Jason Ma joins swyx on-site to unpack how robots can learn new tasks from as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations, why predicting the future of the physical world may be the key to general-purpose robotics, and what it actually takes to build robots that work reliably for real customers. We go deep on Dyna-2, Dyna’s million-hour world-action model that combines future video prediction with robot actions, the scaling laws behind human-to-robot transfer, diffusion transformers and flow matching, and why synthetic environments and self-generated training data could unlock the next wave of robotics progress. Jason also explains why Dyna builds its own hardware instead of relying on off-the-shelf humanoids, how agentic harnesses enable robots to execute hour-long workflows, why dexterous hands and missing sensory data remain major bottlenecks, and what separates real commercial deployments from the graveyard of r…

items.title: China, the FCC, and the Logic of Transceivers
items.content: Quinn has joined the ChinaTalk team after studying semiconductor physics at Yale. Reach out to quinn@chinatalk.media to chat energy, BRI, robots, trade, industrial policy, or anything else! Over the past year, the FCC has released a series of restrictions on foreign-made hardware. First came drones, then routers, and then in July, inverters and robots. The newest devices to be considered are optical transceivers, which convert data into light and back within data centers. Following a Reuters report of a draft ban on new Chinese transceivers, markets responded as if it meant a straightforward substitution of supply, and American optics stocks rose while Chinese optics leaders fell. This swap is not that simple. The FCC’s cybersecurity logic is real but far narrower than the rule suggests. After explaining these gaps, I follow the transceiver supply chain from the module and the laser all the way down to the wafer and the metal it relies on. Chinese companies dominate the top of the stack but are reliant on Western companies in the middle. At the very bottom, Chinese control is ingrained, and the U.S.’s dependence on these basic materials will not be shifted by an FCC rule at the top of the stack. ChinaTalk is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. The Rule On August 4, Reuters reported that the FCC was drafting a ban on import authorization for new models of Chinese optical transceivers to prevent Chinese firms from stealing data, installing malware, or disrupting service. Per the anonymous sources, officials want the rule published and effective by year end, though they cautioned the draft could still be modified or shelved. items.content: Paddy Stephens writes about space, security, and energy for The Wire China , Resilience Media and others. He’s based between London, Nice and Taipei. This is Part 2 of his two-part investigation of China’s Starlink challengers! ChinaTalk is a reader-supported publication. In the first part of this article on China’s responses to Starlink, I analyzed how China views the megaconstellation, and how it might try to disable it in a conflict. This second part reports on China’s mixed record and recent success in building not one but two major low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite megaconstellations of its own. The Chinese government understands Starlink as both a commercial company and a national security asset for the US and partners. Over time, two major ‘Chinese Starlink’ projects have emerged, which between them cover both aspects: Guowang (国网 — literally, “National Network”), a satellite infrastructure provider primarily for the state, and commercially-oriented Qianfan (千帆 — literally, “Thousand Sails”). First to emerge was Guowang, which serves the Chinese state, including the military. It is highly secretive, mentioned by name in few Chinese public policy documents, and public information about it remains scarce. China SatNet 中国星网, the Xiong’an-based state-owned enterprise (SOE) responsible for Guowang, seems to be working closely with the military-industrial complex and state telecommunications companies. The most obvious evidence for this, says Curcio, is China Space Time 中国时空信息集团有限公司, a joint venture between China SatNet, China Mobile, and NORINCO 北方工业, a state-owned defense contractor. items.title: China's Starlink Response
items.content: Paddy Stephens writes about space, security, and energy for The Wire China , Resilience Media and others. He’s based between London, Nice and Taipei. This is Part 1 of his two-part investigation of China’s Starlink challengers! The test lacked the cool confidence of the Falcon 9, SpaceX’s dependable workhorse rocket that slows itself down before landing gently on four legs. Nor was it as elegant as SpaceX’s super-heavy Starship rocket booster, which the company has managed to catch on three occasions with two “chopstick” arms. But as the first stage of the Long March 10B slowed itself into a netted metal box on a sea barge in July this year, the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) joined SpaceX and Bezos’ Blue Origin to become the third entity in the world to have successfully recovered a rocket booster. Long March 10B first stage is collected on a sea barge. Credit: Xinhua . Three soon became four. On its first attempt in December, the booster of the Zhuque-3, a reusable model developed by LandSpace, one of China’s leading commercial rocket companies, ended up as a fireball that smashed spectacularly into the Gobi Desert. Since then, its engineers have clearly been busy. On 18th August, it touched down softly on its extended legs, in size and landing style much like the Falcon 9. The two tests don’t mean China has cracked rocket reusability — it’ll take multiple successful launches of each of the models to prove their reliability. Then it will take more time still to actualize the falling costs and increased launch capacity that reusability has brought SpaceX. Blaine Curcio, the founder of Orbital Gateway Consulting and an authority on China’s space industry, told me that the Long March 10B test is “a meaningful step forward, but the short term impact [on launch capacity] is not huge”. items.title: One year in: How Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore is advancing research, partnership and talent for real-world impact
items.content: On July 24, 2025, Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore (MSRA – Singapore) opened its doors as Microsoft’s first research lab in Southeast Asia. The launch built on more than two decades of collaboration between Microsoft Research Asia and Singapore’s universities, research institutes, and government agencies. It marked a shift to a closer, more integrated relationship aimed at supporting Singapore’s innovation ecosystem and advancing the development and beneficial use of AI. “When we established Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore one year ago, our vision was not simply to open another research lab. It was to build a bridge connecting Microsoft’s frontier AI research with Singapore’s world-class universities, forward-thinking government agencies, and dynamic industry ecosystem. One year in, what gives me the greatest confidence is not just the research we have produced, but the depth of partnership we have built. That is the foundation on which lasting impact is built.” — Dr. Lidong Zhou, corporate vice president at Microsoft and managing director of Microsoft Research Asia Established in 1998, MSRA has a presence in Beijing, Shanghai, Vancouver, and Tokyo, along with Singapore. The Singapore lab strengthens the collaboration with local partners and extends the scientific and societal impact of Microsoft’s global research community.  Over the past year, the Singapore lab has grown its team, deepened partnerships, and explored how frontier AI research can create real-world value. Guided by its mission to advance frontier AI for humanity, its work spans four pillars: next-generation AI models and agentic systems, domain-specific AI for real-world impact, AI-native research practices, and ecosystem and talent development. From frontier research to real-world impact – and back Research has its greatest impact when it moves beyond the laboratory into practice: in health and medicine, enterprises, and the daily oper…
